nameStory: This mint gets its name from the distinctive whorled arrangement of its leaves - they circle around the stem in rings like spokes on a wheel. Despite being called 'mountain mint,' it's not actually restricted to mountains and has a much milder scent than kitchen mints. The 'whorled' part is the key identifier that separates it from its mountain mint cousins.
description: Whorled Mountain Mint is a native perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. It produces clusters of tiny white flowers at the top of square stems, surrounded by whitish or pale green leafy bracts that make the flower heads look frosted. The plant has a subtle minty fragrance when crushed and spreads slowly by underground runners to form small colonies. Like all mints, it has the characteristic square stems and opposite leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in distinctive whorls (circles) of 3-6 around the square stem, with smooth edges and no teeth - this whorled pattern is unique among our mountain mints

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers surrounded by pale, silvery-white bracts that give the whole flower head a frosted appearance in late summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems 1-3 feet tall that are distinctly square when you roll them between your fingers, often branching near the top

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Mild, pleasant minty fragrance when leaves are crushed - much subtler than spearmint or peppermint

habitat: Found in dry to moderately moist open areas including meadows, prairies, old fields, and woodland edges throughout New England. Prefers full sun to partial shade and adapts to various soil types, though it seems to favor slightly alkaline conditions. Often grows alongside goldenrod, asters, and other native wildflowers in sunny meadows.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as square reddish stems with the characteristic whorled leaves becoming visible by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Distinctive whorled foliage is fully developed and easy to spot. Flower buds begin forming in late summer with their pale, frosted appearance.
seasonality.fall: Blooms from August through September with clusters of tiny white flowers. Seeds ripen and disperse by late fall while leaves may turn yellowish.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving dried stems that may persist into winter along with small nutlet seeds scattered nearby.

funFact: Despite having only 6 recorded observations in New England, Whorled Mountain Mint is actually native to the region but has become quite rare - it's like finding a botanical needle in a haystack, making any sighting a real treasure for native plant enthusiasts!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other mountain mints, but the whorled leaf arrangement is a dead giveaway - other mountain mints have simple opposite leaves in pairs, not circles. If you see leaves arranged like spokes around the stem, you've found the whorled species.
contextualKnowledge: Mountain mints aren't true mints (like spearmint or peppermint) and won't overwhelm your garden like their aggressive cousins. They're actually more closely related to oregano and thyme, which explains their milder fragrance and more restrained spreading habit.
compareHints: Unlike its mountain mint relatives that have opposite paired leaves, Whorled Mountain Mint's leaves circle the stem in distinctive whorls. Clustered Mountain Mint has broader, toothed leaves in pairs, while Narrow-leaf Mountain Mint has very thin opposite leaves and a stronger scent. The whorled leaf pattern makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Clustered mountainmint has the most compact, densely rounded flower heads of all the mountainmints - they look like tight white buttons.

Narrowleaf mountainmint stands out from its mountain mint relatives by having the thinnest leaves in the group—often less than 1/4 inch wide compared to the broader leaves of clustered mountainmint or Virginia mountain mint.

Among New England's mountain mints, Virginia mountain mint stands out with its very narrow, lance-shaped leaves - much thinner than the broad leaves of clustered mountain mint or the fuzzy, whitish leaves of hoary mountain mint.
Among the mountainmints, hoary mountainmint is easily distinguished by its uniquely fuzzy, silvery appearance - the other species have green, relatively smooth leaves.
Torrey's mountainmint differs from its more common relatives like Virginia mountain mint by its narrower leaves and denser flower clusters.
